introduction: This guide begins where John’s Gospel begins: the Word already was, so the station of a Manifestation of God is not conferred at a baptism or a public hour but is His from a beginning that has no beginning. Its readings then gather the signs of childhood, the knowledge that no school gave, the images of being roused from sleep, and a closing admission that the nature of such consciousness is not known to us. The company set beside them has told both stories. Jeremiah is known before he is formed, Wisdom is set up from everlasting, and Jesus says “Before Abraham was, I am”; but Amos was a herdman taken from the flock, Moses pleads that he cannot speak, the boy Samuel does not recognise the voice, and the Qur’an tells its Prophet that he once knew not what the Scripture was. Luke, who shows the boy astonishing the teachers, also says that he grew in wisdom. Plato and Wordsworth widen the question to every soul.
questions: John has Jesus speak of a glory “before the world was”, and Matthew describes the Spirit descending at the baptism. How do the readings ask us to hold these two together?

Amos, Moses and the boy Samuel each experience the call as something that arrives. What would it mean to say their dignity was nonetheless “inborn”, and where does the comparison with a Manifestation stop?
The teachers in the temple are astonished at a boy’s answers, and Jerusalem asks “How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?” What do the readings make of knowledge that no school explains?
Bahá’u’lláh writes of being roused from slumber, and the Qur’an says “Did He not find thee wandering?” How can language of awakening be read beside statements of awareness from the beginning?
The guide ends with “we do not know”, and Deuteronomy with “the secret things belong unto the Lord”. What is gained by leaving the question there?

outside.why: The reading denies that Christ’s station began at the baptism. In John’s Gospel Jesus himself prays of a glory he had “before the world was”.
Matthew tells the baptism as an event: the heavens open and the Spirit descends like a dove. Does the scene record a beginning, or disclose what was already so?

“A Prophet from the beginning that hath no beginning.” Jeremiah hears something near it of himself: known, sanctified and ordained before he was formed, though his scope is one prophet’s calling and not an eternal station.

Amos tells the opposite story of himself: no prophet nor prophet’s son, a herdman whom the Lord took from following the flock. Is a call that arrives in mid-life another kind of prophethood, or the same act of God seen from below?
“From childhood the signs of greatness are clearly manifested.” Luke’s one scene of the boy Jesus has the teachers astonished at his understanding and answers.
The same chapter of Luke says the boy increased in wisdom and stature. What the reading leaves open is how awareness from the beginning sits with growth of any kind.
It was acknowledged that Bahá’u’lláh had entered no school, yet the learned brought him their questions. The same puzzle is voiced in Jerusalem: “How knoweth this man letters, having never learned?”
The burden of prophethood is “inborn”, not conferred. Paul, an apostle and no Manifestation, still says he was set apart from his mother’s womb, and yet dates the revealing to a later day.
Moses at the bush pleads that he is not eloquent and never was, and has to be promised a mouth. Can a dignity be inborn and still be felt, by the one who carries it, as a burden laid on from outside?
The sun “does not draw its light from other sources”, and the world receives its light from the divine teachers. John calls the Word the true Light which lights every one who comes into the world.
He “never attended school nor learned of men”. The Qur’an names its own messenger the Prophet who can neither read nor write, and makes of that a sign.

The Master’s knowledge must be “innate and spontaneous and not acquired”. Plato’s Socrates makes all learning a recollection in every soul. What is left of the distinction if everyone’s knowledge is innate?
Perfections “innate, not acquired”, a light heavenly and not earthly. Wisdom in Proverbs speaks as one possessed by the Lord before his works of old, set up from everlasting.
All else “hath been created through the potency of My word”. John’s prologue says of the Word that all things were made by him, and without him was not any thing made.
Bahá’u’lláh speaks of being roused from slumber by the Breeze of God. The Qur’an tells Muhammad that a Spirit was inspired in him, and that before it he knew not what the Scripture was.
“Did He not find thee wandering and direct thee?” The verse describes a before and an after in the Prophet’s own life. How is such language to be read beside a station that has no beginning?
Before the creative Word is uttered “the world existed but none had knowledge of Him”. “Before Abraham was, I am” claims the same priority of being over being known.

The Manifestations “were aware before the Revelation”. The boy Samuel is called three times and does not know who is calling until Eli tells him. Here is prophetic awareness that has to be taught its own name.

“We set foot within the School of God when ye lay slumbering.” Wordsworth gives every child a home before birth, from which each comes trailing clouds of glory and then forgets. What distinguishes the one who does not forget?
In the prayer it is the worshipper who lay asleep “on the bed of self” and was wakened by a voice. The early Christian hymn Paul quotes calls every sleeper to the same rising.
“I sleep, but my heart waketh.” The Song knows a sleep in which the hearer already listens for the beloved’s voice, which may be the nearest image for an awakening that is not a first knowing.
“What the nature of that consciousness was we do not know.” Deuteronomy draws the same line: the secret things belong to God, and what is revealed is given for doing.

quran-knewest-not-the-scripture.text: And thus have We inspired in thee (Muhammad) a Spirit of Our command. Thou knewest not what the Scripture was, nor what the Faith. But We have made it a light whereby We guide whom We will of Our bondmen. And lo! thou verily dost guide unto a right path,

luke-child-grew.text: And the child grew, and waxed strong in spirit, filled with wisdom: and the grace of God was upon him
